sentences.text: In January 1962, at a girls' boarding school in Tanganyika, three students started laughing.
And they could not stop.
There was no joke.
Nobody knew what was so funny.
Then a classmate caught it.
Then another.
Within weeks, ninety-five of the school's one hundred and fifty-nine pupils were laughing, crying, or fainting.
And the teachers?
Not a single giggle.
They just watched nobody concentrate on a single lesson.
In March, the school closed and sent the girls home.
Bad idea.
The laughter went home with them.
In the village of Nshamba, two hundred and seventeen people, mostly young, had laughing attacks.
It jumped to other schools.
In the end, fourteen of them had to close.
It took about eighteen months to fade away completely.
Today, experts call it mass hysteria: stress that spreads from person to person, like a yawn across a room.
The country had just become independent, and the students felt huge pressure from teachers and parents.
In all, around a thousand people were affected.
Because laughter really is contagious, even when nothing is funny.
